headline: Four mail listeners dispatched a pipelined command against the state as it stood before the previous one finished
summary:
A POP3 client that wrote `USER a`, `PASS a`, `USER b`, `PASS b` in one segment authenticated twice. The guards that refuse a second login read the session stage, and the stage moves only after the credential check resolves, while the reader dispatched every complete line it held without waiting for any of them. All four lines were answered against the state as it stood before the first check finished.

The reader now takes one command, waits for it, and then takes the next. Four listeners shared the shape and all four are fixed; the SMTP listener already worked this way. Alongside it: a retention floor that measured age from a date the sender chose, a STARTTLS upgrade that verified an address-literal peer against `localhost`, and every listener silently accepting option names it does not have.

items.title: A pipelined second credential pair no longer authenticates
items.body:
`b.mail.server.pop3` refuses a second `USER`/`PASS` pair on a session that is already authenticating. It did not: the AUTHORIZATION-state guards read the session stage and the actor, and `PASS` sets both only after the credential check resolves. The reader dispatched every complete line in its buffer without waiting, so a client that wrote both pairs in a single segment had all four answered while the stage was still AUTHORIZATION and the actor still empty. Both pairs were verified concurrently and both entered TRANSACTION.

The reader now takes one command, waits for it to finish, then takes the next. `b.mail.server.imap` and `b.mail.server.managesieve` read the same way and are changed with it; `b.mail.server.mx` already chained its input and is unchanged. Any guard that reads state a later handler writes was unsound in all three, not only the credential pair.

`b.mail.server.submission` holds the client's pipelined remainder on a pending-command flag instead, and already did so for the sender-policy hook. It did not for `AUTH`, so two credential exchanges written in one segment were verified at the same time on a session that was not authenticated yet. The flag is now held there too, set before the verify begins and released on every path.

Waiting for a handler only works if the handler hands its work back, and most did not: they started their work and returned nothing, so the reader had nothing to wait for and took the next command immediately. Every command handler in the three listeners now returns what it starts. The nesting is the part worth naming: POP3's `PASS` did return its credential check, but the session leaves AUTHORIZATION inside a further step that opens the mailbox, so waiting for the check alone still read the next command against a session that was not authenticated yet. That step is returned too, and so is the result of the shared SASL round.

One consequence is visible on the wire: a command that arrives while the previous one is still running is read after it finishes, not during. It is still answered, and a second login is still refused; the refusal now names the state the session actually reached.

Because commands wait, a connection holds more than one at a time, and the limits follow. The line cap applies to a line, checked where a line is taken, so a client that pipelines several short commands is no longer answered `BAD Line too long` for their combined size. What a line cap cannot bound is how many lines are held: `b.mail.server.imap`, `.pop3` and `.managesieve` each accept eight lines' worth of pipelined commands and close the connection past that, so a peer cannot hold a slow handler open and keep sending.

A handler that rejects is answered once, by the listener that already owned that reply, and the connection closes on an error the reader itself raises.

items.title: A retention floor measures arrival, not a date the sender picked
items.body:
`b.mail.agent.expunge` decides whether a message is old enough to destroy from `receivedAt`, and refuses when that is absent. It used to fall back to `internalDate`, which the sender chooses: RFC 9051 section 6.3.12 lets an APPEND carry a date-time, and a backend that records it without stamping its own arrival time produces a row whose only date came from the client. A row dated to the epoch cleared a floor of any size, so an account that can APPEND could date a message into the past and then destroy it inside the window the floor exists to hold.

A missing `receivedAt` is now unknown arrival whatever `internalDate` says, and unknown arrival already refuses. `internalDate` is unchanged for display and for `INTERNALDATE` responses; it is not an input to a destruction decision.

The store that ships stamps both fields with server time, so this was reachable through a backend that honours the APPEND date.

items.title: STARTTLS names the peer it is verifying
items.body:
`b.mail.send` over STARTTLS sets the peer host on the upgraded connection, as the implicit-TLS path already did. Without it, node checks the certificate against `servername || host`, and `servername` is deliberately left undefined for an address literal because an IP is not a valid SNI name. With neither set the check fell back to node's default and verified the peer against `localhost`, so a server presenting a correct IP SAN could not be verified at all.

This was the only client-side upgrade over an existing socket in the framework.

items.title: Every mail listener refuses an option name it does not have
items.body:
`b.mail.server.mx.create`, `.submission.create`, `.imap.create`, `.pop3.create` and `.managesieve.create` throw `mail-server-<name>/bad-opts` naming the unknown key and listing the accepted ones. They accepted anything: a misspelled option left the setting at its default while the caller believed it was set, and afterwards nothing distinguished a typo from an omission. These options decide security posture, so the failure was silent in the direction that matters.

Upgrade note: a call passing a name that was never read now throws where it used to start a listener. That is the point, and the message names the key.

Two names were only ever accepted, never read. `compress` appeared in a source comment describing how to enable COMPRESS=DEFLATE; nothing read it, and the extension is not offered because a compression oracle applies to the encrypted stream. `maxSize` and `depth` are parsed from a GETMETADATA command, not from construction.

items.title: The vendored `@blamejs/pki` bundle moves to 0.6.21
items.body:
`b.mtlsCa` and `b.auth.passkey` are built on the vendored PKI toolkit; `lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` and its `MANIFEST.json` hashes now carry 0.6.21. The toolkit is internal and is not re-exported, so no blamejs API changes shape.

Two of the fixes in the range harden lookups against a supplied name. A Sigstore bundle whose certificate holds a non-text subjectAltName `otherName` value is no longer read as an identity, so a value whose raw bytes matched a pinned identity can no longer satisfy an identity policy; and an algorithm, curve, digest or profile name that collides with an inherited object property is refused with the verb's own error rather than reaching the lookup. The rest adds CMS composite ML-KEM recipients and the SCEP `getCert`, `getCrl` and CertRep verbs, none of which the framework calls.

The vendored public-suffix list is refreshed to its 2026-09-01 snapshot, which is what `b.cookies` and the origin checks read when deciding registrable domain boundaries.

items.title: `audit` reaches the sink on the listeners that document it
items.body: `b.mail.server.imap`, `.pop3` and `.managesieve` document an `audit` option and never read it, so an operator who wired a sink received nothing from these three. The sink is now validated at construction, in the same shape every other primitive takes, and receives each event alongside the framework audit rather than in place of it.

items.title: An IMAP literal carries the rest of its own command line
items.body:
The reader consumed a literal's octets and left the CRLF that ends the command line in the buffer, where the next turn read it as a line of its own. An empty command is refused, so a client that completed an APPEND correctly was answered `BAD` after the command had already succeeded.

The bytes after the octets are now read as the rest of that command, whatever the literal's length; a zero-length literal is treated like any other. When nothing follows, the literal was the last argument and reaches the handler as bytes, which is unchanged and is the only way to carry a value that is not text.

A synchronizing literal is answered with a continuation request whatever its length, a zero-byte one included, and the minimum-arrival-rate guard no longer applies to a literal that carries no octets. A client following the specification waits for that `+` before sending the line terminator, so an empty literal that was never answered left both sides waiting.

What follows the octets is what says whether the literal was the last argument, so the reader waits for that line to end rather than deciding from whichever bytes arrived together. RFC 9051 puts the terminator in the command's own grammar, so it is always coming. Deciding on an empty receive buffer would decide on TCP segmentation: `LOGIN {5}` and its octets, split from the arguments that follow, would complete as a whole command with the arguments it had, which for a login is a session authenticated on a fragment. A command now parses the same however it was split.

When something does follow, the literal was not the last token, which RFC 9051 allows wherever an astring is allowed and the `LOGIN` example in section 6.2.3 uses twice on one line. Those bytes continue the command: the body is written back into the line as a quoted string and the line is read again, so a second literal opens the way the first did and a command may carry any number of them.

After a literal's octets the grammar allows the end of the line or a space and more arguments. Anything else is refused, rather than read as this command's arguments, so a client that does not terminate its line cannot have its next command absorbed into the previous one.

A literal's bytes are not charged against the listener's `maxLineBytes`. The wire frames the two separately: that option bounds what arrives as one line, while a literal is framed by its own octet count and bounded by `maxLiteralBytes`, so a short command carrying a large argument is no longer refused as a long line. What the literals of one command may add up to is bounded in turn, since a command may carry any number of them, and the last one counts toward that total like the rest. A literal may also be an element of a parenthesized list, where the byte after its octets is the closing paren rather than a space, and that reads as the command it is. A literal that is written back into the command still passes the profile's own command-line cap, which is what bounds how much command text is parsed at all.

A literal that is not the last token is refused when its body cannot be written back as a quoted string: one carrying CR, LF or NUL, or one whose octets are not decodable as UTF-8. A literal carries CHAR8 and need not be text at all, and decoding what is not UTF-8 substitutes a replacement character for each byte it cannot read, which would hand the command a password the client never sent and fail the login as a wrong one. The command is refused, naming the reason, rather than rebuilt into something else. A literal in the last position is never decoded and is unaffected, which is why a password or a search term sent as one still arrives exactly as it was written.

A client that sends a literal's octets and no line terminator now waits, as it does for any unfinished line.

items.title: Tearing a connection down stops the reader that was serving it
items.body:
All five mail listeners close the session, not just the socket. Closing is what marks the session, and that marker is the only thing standing between a torn-down connection and the commands the peer had already queued behind the handler that was running.

`b.mail.server.pop3` and `.managesieve` wire the post-STARTTLS teardown separately from the plaintext one and passed it the upgraded socket alone, so an idle timeout there left the reader believing the session was live: a `DELE` pipelined behind a `STAT` reached the maildrop after the connection was gone.

`b.mail.server.submission` keeps the client's pipelined remainder in its buffer and resumes reading it when a pending command answers. A refused backlog destroyed the socket and left that buffer, so a `MAIL` / `RCPT` / `BDAT ... LAST` queued behind an `AUTH` reached message finalization on a connection the server had already refused.

`b.mail.server.mx` chains each arriving segment behind the previous one and skips the queue once the connection closes, but the flag it reads was written from the socket's own close event. That event arrives a turn later than the queued segment resumes, so a segment that arrived while a gate was still running was processed after the gate tore the connection down.

A session also ends without the listener deciding it, and those paths run no refusal: a peer that pipelines commands behind a slow one and then hangs up, or a socket the server destroys at shutdown. `b.mail.server.imap`, `.managesieve` and `.submission` mark the session on the socket's own close too, so a handler settling afterwards finds the session already over rather than executing what the peer left queued.

The marker is a field of its own rather than a session-stage value, because the stage is the protocol position and handlers assign it: a close landing while a login or a sender check was in flight would otherwise be overwritten when that check answered.

Every POP3 TRANSACTION handler also hands its store call back to the reader. `STAT`, `LIST`, `RETR`, `DELE`, `RSET`, `TOP`, `UIDL` and the UPDATE-state commit registered their work for the session-end wait and returned nothing, so the reader took the next command while the previous one was still in the store.

items.title: A ManageSieve literal is refused rather than repaired when it is not UTF-8
items.body:
`b.mail.server.managesieve` decoded the octets of a `PUTSCRIPT` literal with a conversion that substitutes a replacement character for every byte it cannot read. The substitution happened before anything examined the value, so the script that was validated and stored was a repaired copy: a `0xFF` inside a comment came back as three octets, the stored script was longer than the count the client announced, and the reply was `OK`.

A Sieve script decides what is filed, forwarded and discarded, so a byte altered inside a string, a header name or an address changes what a rule does rather than only how it reads. RFC 5804 section 2.3 requires the script to be verified before it is accepted, and verifying the repaired copy is not verifying what arrived. Such a script is now refused, naming the reason, and nothing reaches the store.

The same conversion ran on an `AUTHENTICATE` initial response sent as a literal. A SASL token is base64, and the replacement character's own bytes fall outside that alphabet, so they are dropped when the token is decoded: two different responses on the wire reached the verifier as one credential. That round is refused too.

items.title: A literal that arrives with its own opener is not pipelined data
items.body:
The listeners bound how much command text may wait while a handler runs. A literal's payload is not waiting: it belongs to the command whose opener announced it, and what bounds it is the literal cap, or for ManageSieve the profile's script cap.

That bound read only the transfer already recorded on the session, and a client that writes an opener and its payload in one segment has not started one yet, so the payload was charged as backlog. `b.mail.server.managesieve` answered `NO` and closed the connection on a `PUTSCRIPT` well inside the profile's script cap, and `b.mail.server.imap` did the same for a literal sent behind a queued command. Whether a script was accepted depended on how the client's write was split.

Both listeners now exempt the declared payload already present in the buffer. What counts as an opener is what the listener's own command parser says opens a literal, so a line that is not a command it has (`BOGUS {1048576+}`) buys no allowance for the bytes behind it. Only one payload is exempt, the first the scan reaches: the reader takes one command at a time, so a second literal pipelined behind the first is waiting, and bytes after the exempt payload are charged as before.

Whether the session is authenticated is not part of that question. A client may pipeline the login and the literal command in one write, and judging the second against the state as it stood before the first refuses a command that is valid by the time the reader reaches it.

That makes the exemption a prediction about a line the reader has not taken. When the reader takes it and refuses the literal, those octets are ordinary queue, so the allowance is applied again per command rather than only when the socket next delivers data, which a single coalesced write never does.

items.title: A command handler must hand its work back to the reader
items.body:
A listener that reads one command at a time is only serialized if its handlers return what they start. A handler that begins asynchronous work as a bare statement returns nothing, the reader has nothing to wait for, and it takes the next command immediately — which is the race the serialization exists to remove, still present on every path except the one that was fixed by hand.

The check refuses that shape in the mail listeners. It names the files that read differently and why: the submission listener holds its buffer on a pending-command flag rather than on a returned promise, and two others read an HTTP request body rather than a command stream.

items.title: Growth measurements share one implementation
items.body:
Eight assertions across five suites timed a scan at two input sizes and divided. Each held its own sample count and its own floor, and at sub-millisecond readings the ratio reports what else the machine was doing: one of them measured 9.5x for 4x input on a shared runner for a scan that measures 3.4x to 4.2x locally.

They now use the shared measurement the framework already had, which declines to take a ratio at all below a floor where a quadratic scan would already have taken seconds, and re-measures with more samples before failing anything.

A ninth was left behind by that sweep, because it measures a protocol round trip and the shared measurement only accepted synchronous work. It kept a single unrepeated reading and failed a run at 9.41 against a bound of 9, on a scan that is linear. The measurement now has an asynchronous form, and a check refuses a ratio taken by hand so the next one cannot be missed by enumeration.

items.title: The mail listeners have live coverage
items.body:
The release gate ran the mail backend's live tests on any change under `lib/mail-server*`, and those tests exercised the SMTP client, DKIM and S/MIME. None of them opened a connection to the IMAP, POP3, ManageSieve or submission listeners, so a change to all five reported a green live run that had not reached them.

A new integration file drives the four listeners over real sockets with certificate verification on, against the shipped mail store on a real database rather than a stand-in, and relays a submitted message onward by SMTP so the delivery assertion is what a receiving server got. It runs whenever a listener changes.

items.title: A `var` read above its own assignment is refused
items.body:
A `var` read before the line that assigns it holds `undefined` rather than raising, so the expression around it yields a value and execution continues with it. A listener option resolved from a profile name assigned eight lines lower took a fallback and bounded literals at the strict number on a permissive listener.

The check refuses a read evaluated in the same scope as the declaration, across `lib/`, `scripts/` and `test/`. A read inside a nested function is left alone: that runs when the function is called, which is after the assignment, and it is the form the codebase uses throughout.
